context.hint: The policy-local decoder passed a multi-attribute robustness matrix, but it still accepted only semicolon-terminated references. An HTML tokenizer consumes the longest possible run of decimal or hex digits and treats the trailing semicolon as optional, so a decimal reference such as &#106avascript: resolves to j plus avascript: even without a semicolon. The serializer escapes an unrecognized ampersand in that form, which reduces the practical impact, but the policy comparison remains inconsistent with parser semantics. The next step is to implement numeric-reference termination faithfully and bound the compatibility cost for invalid values.
context.surface: Python library made of a streaming HTML tokenizer, an attribute policy filter and an entity-preserving serializer. Untrusted markup enters through a sanitize API configured with allowed tags, allowed attributes and allowed URI schemes.
assumptions: The attacker controls the entire untrusted HTML fragment but not the sanitizer configuration or the local filesystem.
Allowed attributes include at least one URI-valued attribute on a link, an image, a video poster, a form action, a cite/background attribute and an SVG link.
The sanitizer's protocol list is configurable; http, https and mailto are allowed by default and a caller may add a custom scheme.
All experiments use a disposable local Python environment and in-memory strings; no network service or public target is involved.
The official benchmark evaluator is external; local test results are not an official pass.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: decoding every named and numeric HTML character reference for the URI policy comparison will remove entity-hidden disallowed schemes, because the serializer keeps the original reference spelling while the policy sees the resolved scheme. Prerequisite: a policy-local decoder built from the parser's named-entity table plus decimal and hexadecimal numeric parsing. Bounded test: sanitize link attributes containing hex, decimal, uppercase-hex, named-colon, named-tab, named-newline and numeric-control variants of javascript: and file:, then compare against allowed http(s), mailto, relative, query-ampersand and custom-protocol controls. Expected result: all entity-hidden disallowed values lose the URI attribute; allowed and relative values keep their exact serialized bytes. Falsifier: any entity-hidden scheme survives, or any allowed control changes bytes. Cleanup: revert the one policy line and helper in the disposable copy; limitations: the comparison value is decoded but the emitted value intentionally stays encoded.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: an attacker can hide a disallowed scheme behind a numeric character reference without a trailing semicolon, which the current decoder leaves intact because it only matches terminated references. Prerequisite: a policy decoder that can consume a maximal digit run. Bounded test: sanitize a link with &#106avascript: plus a plain javascript: control, then also test zero-padded and uppercase-hex variants; record whether the URI attribute remains. Expected result: the repaired decoder consumes decimal or hex digits greedily, optionally consumes one semicolon, resolves the value, and removes the attribute. Falsifier: any no-semicolon form still resolves to a blocked scheme after the repair. Cleanup: revert one helper. Limitations: greedy consumption must not turn a legitimate reference-lookalike into a different scheme.

Hypothesis: out-of-range, empty or surrogate numeric references can raise during character conversion or cause over-rejection, turning a robustness fix into a compatibility regression. Prerequisite: numeric parsing with explicit invalid-value handling. Bounded test: sanitize link values containing an empty numeric reference, a value above the Unicode maximum, a surrogate and a zero code point; compare emitted bytes with the pristine snapshot and verify no exception. Expected result: no exception and unchanged control bytes; invalid references are left for the policy view because a browser maps them to a replacement character that cannot form a scheme. Falsifier: any exception or control drift. Cleanup: remove the cases. Limitations: replacement-character behavior may differ by parser version.

Hypothesis: hexadecimal references with mixed case, a leading x/X and zero padding, with or without a semicolon, exercise the same termination rule and should be covered alongside decimal. Prerequisite: the same numeric decoder. Bounded test: sanitize uppercase-X, lowercase-x, zero-padded and short hex forms, including a hex run that consumes the leading a of avascript and therefore is not the javascript scheme; compare relative and allowed controls. Expected result: forms resolving to javascript: are removed; the over-consuming hex form stays a non-scheme and keeps its bytes. Falsifier: a surviving javascript: form or a changed control. Cleanup: none beyond the fixture. Limitations: exact code-point mapping can vary for invalid values.

Hypothesis: named references beyond colon and tab, such as newline, slash, question mark, percent or number, could assemble or break URI values differently from numeric parsing because named tables are case-sensitive. Prerequisite: full named-entity decoding. Bounded test: sanitize a table of named references inside otherwise allowed relative and query values, and named references inside disallowed scheme prefixes; compare bytes with the pristine snapshot. Expected result: disallowed schemes are removed and ordinary query/relative values are unchanged. Falsifier: a named reference changes an allowed control or assembles a surviving blocked scheme. Cleanup: remove the table fixture. Limitations: very large entity alphabets are mostly repeated coverage.

evaluations.rationale: Retained incumbent. Its named-entity repair is the base, but the round-2 matrix proved it incomplete for numeric-reference termination.
Selected. Names the exact observed gap and prescribes a bounded parser-faithful termination rule with a clear falsifier.
Deferred but incorporated as the invalid-reference control. Important compatibility guard, not the primary repair.
Deferred as regression coverage. Correctly extends the numeric concern to hex and over-consumption controls.
Deferred. Useful named-entity and query-string coverage, weaker discrimination than the demonstrated numeric gap.

observation.summary: Extended the policy decoder with HTML-tokenizer numeric termination: an optional x/X prefix selects hexadecimal, the longest decimal or hex digit run is consumed, and a trailing semicolon is optional. Decimal &#106avascript:, zero-padded decimal, terminated decimal/hex and uppercase-X forms now lose the URI attribute. Forms resolving to an allowed scheme or a relative reference keep their existing bytes, and a hex run that consumes the leading a is correctly not the javascript scheme. Invalid, zero and surrogate code points are left untouched for the policy view so malformed controls keep their bytes; a browser maps them to a replacement character and cannot form a scheme from them. The full local suite passed (256 tests, 2 expected failures), including 22 focused entity-URI checks. Evidence strength: direct local result plus parser-semantics controls. Limitation: the official evaluator remains external.
observation.next_hint: Run one consolidated end-to-end matrix that re-parses every emitted URI attribute with the same HTML parser, and apply only the source delta to a fresh copy before exporting the official patch JSONL.
